Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen Anthony Albanese embraces Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian foreign policy ‘My friend’: Anthony Albanese announces $60m more for Ukraine at Zelenskyy meeting An emotional prime minister says that Kyiv’s cause is ‘an issue for the world’ as he also sets out the need for a new global order Martin Farrer Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anthony Albanese has announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN meeting in New York. With the prime minister planning to use a key speech in New York to warn that the international world order was “no longer fit for purpose”, he hugged the Ukrainian president as the latter thanked Australia for its support. ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club Read more Albanese became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression. “[His] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said. “Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is that the people of Ukraine were underestimated.” The two leaders signed a 10-year bilateral security agreement which will lead to an extra $45m in Australian Defence Force equipment for Ukraine. A further $10m will go to Ukraine’s energy support fund, while $5m will be spent on humanitarian assistance. The $60m fund will bring Australia’s total contribution to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in 2022 to $1.9bn. As part of the agreement, Australia will also step up training to help Ukrainian forces deter and repel any future Russian attacks. It will also look to explore co-operation for training centres and jointly produce air-defence measures, missiles and drones. The prime minister said the agreement was a proud day for Australians in seeking to uphold international laws. “This is an issue not just for Europe, this is an issue for the world,” Albanese told reporters in New York upon signing the agreement. “If a large, more powerful country in Russia is allowed to profit from breaking the international rules of law with its illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine, then that sets a bad precedent for the entire world.” Albanese said the bilateral agreement would be in place not only during the war in Ukraine, but during peacetime once the conflict concludes. Zelenskyy said the agreement was the “strongest document between our countries”, and would increase trade and security. “It’s all for our people, for the security,” he said. It was a busy day of diplomacy for Albanese, who was addressing the Atlantic Council with a major speech on foreign policy and also signed a new strategic partnership with the Netherlands, seeking to boost defence ties and secure justice for the victims of MH17. In his speech, the prime minister was expected to say that the international world order set up following the second world war was no longer fit for purpose and that institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges. The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment. “Since the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed,” he will say. “Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged. “The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.” Australian Associated Press also contributed to this report. https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-featur.text: Auto Features Follow us Skoda Kylaq Pune to Prague Leg 2: Prague calling Driving through Central Asia on the ancient Silk Route, crossing continents by bridge and taking in the history of Europe. Welcome to part 2 of our mega Pune-to-Prague drive in a Skoda Kylaq. Jay Patil recounts the journey. 11 min read • 4 Oct '26 Jay Patil In the previous issue (August 2026), you saw the Skoda Kylaq take on the familiarity of India, the hills and traditions of Nepal, and the variety of China through Tibet’s gorgeous but bone-shaking terrain, followed by the sensory overload of food and culture. Now, it was time for a fresh experience through Central Asia on the ancient Silk Route, subsequently entering Europe towards our final destination. Kyrgyzstan – Uzbekistan – Kazakhstan Kyrgyzstan The Kylaq had everyone turning heads. Crossing the Chinese border into Kyrgyzstan was like crossing into a different world. The differences are immediate, right from the signage, fonts and faces to the sights, terrain and traffic. Being a landlocked country peppered with alpine mountains, one doesn’t need to go far to experience what Kyrgyzstan has to offer. As you drive through the ribbon of tarmac between the peaks, you realise why it is called the “Switzerland of Asia”. A roughly 400km drive to our first halt in Naryn was smooth sailing. However, the chilly weather was a far cry from the piercing heat of China. We pulled out our jackets that were buried deep in our bags and made a beeline the next day for the capital city of Bishkek. The roads are a driver’s delight, and while there aren’t many sights to stop and admire, the Orto-Tokoy Reservoir made for a stunning photo-op. Kyrgyzstan in numbers Distance covered 1,321km Fuel consumed 126.49 litres Average fuel economy 10.44kpl Approximate fuel cost Rs 11,727 Average per-litre fuel cost Rs 92.58 Total time driven 34hrs 23min Average speed 38.4kph From Bishkek, we headed to Osh, which is also known as the capital of the south and is the oldest city in Kyrgyzstan. Walking through the Jayma Bazaar in the city centre, you may get a bit of celebrity treatment, as the locals aren’t used to having many tourists just walking through. Some playful heckling and wide smiles add to the overall experience. Chorsu Bazaar is a one-stop shop for everything in Tashkent. What the market offers is mounds of kurut, a snack made from curdled milk or oghurt, salted and then hardened. The best part is its extended shelf life without needing a refrigerator. We packed some with the hope of eating it at home, knowing fully well that it would vanish by the next town. From Osh, we would be exiting the stunning valleys and terrain of Kyrgyzstan and entering the city of Fergana in Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan Registan Square in Samarkand is breathtaking from every angle. Like Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan also has its own personality. While there are similarities in the faces and fashion, the city of Fergana has a tinge of European infrastructure. Roads are lined with trees and patir shops – flatbread made from butter or lamb fat, with intricate detailing and some sesame seeds sprinkled on top. It’s pretty enough to dissuade you from eating it, but tastes like something that would go extremely well with a cup of chai. Uzbekistan in numbers Distance covered 1,257km Fuel consumed 81.74 litres Average fuel economy 15.37kpl Approximate fuel cost Rs 9,800 Average per-litre fuel cost Rs 120 Total time driven 27hrs 5min Average speed 46.4kph What is also fascinating is the number of old Soviet-era cars still running on the highways with no fuss. We shared road space with old Ladas crammed with luggage inside and on the roof. Over the smooth highways of Uzbekistan, the Kylaq had an easy run, allowing us to focus on the sights around us. From Fergana, we headed to the capital city of Tashkent. A properly modern metropolis with high-end malls and low-slung supercars, parks, walkways and everything you expect from a big city. So, to get a taste of age-old tradition, we ventured towards Samarkand, which used to be a major trading hub on the Silk Route. The Shah-i-Zinda ensemble has 11 mausoleums with incredibly detailed azure and turquoise tiles. Entering Samarkand, you almost feel the tradition in the air. Years of cross-cultural civilisation have made it a stunning destination to get a glimpse of history, and it is unlike any other Western or Eastern city. The highlight here, of course, is the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in the Registan ensemble. Turquoise domes kissing the sky, with walls adorned with hand-carved artistry, are nothing short of breathtaking. You can walk through the corridors and the square innumerable times, and each time, you will gasp at the sheer detail and effort. And to think it was built as far back as the 15th century. Magnificent is an understatement. After soaking in the stunning detail, we headed back to Tashkent and straight to the equally fascinating Chorsu Bazaar. What looks like an IMAX dome on the outside is a full-fledged one-stop shop on the inside. Teas, dry fruits or even a leg of lamb, you can get it all here. Uzbekistan’s market is nothing short of paradise for tea lovers. After a long walk that ended with bags of tea and dehydrated kiwis, we headed for Uzbekistan’s pièce de résistance: the famous plov. Like a biryani, but made with different spices, and if you want to go heavy on culture, you can have one with horse meat, too. Some bravehearts did try it and resorted to chicken or lamb, but it did offer the lost taste of biryani and got us homesick in the first bite. Massive dome known as a kazan used to make the famous Uzbek plov. After days of driving through mountains and around lakes, and walking through corridors that were once at the peak of world trade, our next adventure would take us to the Great Steppe of Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan The Great Steppe in Kazakhstan feels like driving on an endless treadmill. Crossing from Turkmenistan after vigorous checks, Kazakhstan feels almost desolate. Arrow-straight highways for kilometres, between acres of flat land with nothing on the horizon. We were driving through green pastures that would turn into brown, dried patches before turning green again, kilometre after kilometre. The Great Steppe, while stunning in size, is also a bit monotonous when you’re driving through it for days. The only respite would be a herd of double-humped Bactrian camels, cooling off at a nearby pond and often curious to know what a cherry-red Kylaq was doing in the middle of Kazakhstan. At Rs 58.17 per litre, Kazakhstan offered the lowest fuel price of the entire drive. An interesting stop between Turkistan and Aral is the Baikonur Cosmodrome, which is the world’s first and largest operational space launch facility. However, thanks to the endless highways through Aral, Aktobe and Atyrau, we only got to test the Kylaq’s wheel alignment and its highway stability more than we would have liked. Baikonur Cosmodrome – the world’s first, largest and operational space launch facility. The mighty Stans were all about breathtaking sights, warm people and mouth-watering cuisine. The region still feels unadulterated, and that itself is what makes it special. Kazakhstan in numbers Distance covered 3,237km Fuel consumed 229.52 litres Average fuel economy 14.10kpl Approximate fuel cost Rs 13,325 Average per-litre fuel cost Rs 58.17 Total time driven 42hrs Average speed 77.1kph Georgia – The Birthplace of Wine Compared to the vast landscapes and long highways of the Stans, Georgia was a contradiction. Based within the Caucasus Mountains, it has its share of twisties, which the Kylaq enjoyed. But the capital, Tbilisi, is the largest city and thereby pretty chaotic to drive in. Peak-hour traffic is just like what you would have in India, so we parked the car in a worryingly narrow alleyway and, for the most part, made our way on foot. Huge statue of the founder of Tbilisi King Vakhtang I Gorgasali. Like any big city, Tbilisi has its modern side, with glass buildings and modern restaurants, but there is still a large section that is rooted in tradition. Cobblestone streets with wooden houses and sulphur baths are a fascinating experience, as is the fantastic view from near the monument of King Vakhtang Gorgasali, the founder of Tbilisi. The monument itself is a striking bronze equestrian statue located on a rocky cliff above the Mtkvari River, next to the historic Metekhi Church in Tbilisi, Georgia. But Georgia is known to be the birthplace of wine, and on our drive to Tbilisi, we spotted several vineyards sprawling for acres. We had to get a closer look, and thankfully, our guide’s friend owned one of them. Georgian wine fermented in clay jars buried in the ground. The Georgians still use the ancient process of fermenting wine in barrels under the floor, but have now blended it with modern technology that allows them to control the temperature and get a more consistent batch each time. Wine connoisseur or not, the experience is enthralling. Khachapuri (flatbread with cheese and egg) is Georgia’s national snack. The city tour built up an appetite, and we followed the scent of fresh bread for some authentic khachapuri. A Georgian flatbread that is hollowed out in the centre and filled with cheese, khachapuri varies depending on the region you’re in. You can have it with an egg cracked into it or with meat, too. Coastal city of Batumi is a stark contrast of Tbilisi. With sightseeing done, we drove the next day to the coastal city of Batumi. A vibrant, modern city with a lot more European influence. However, if the roads in Tbilisi were narrow, Batumi was on another level. Despite the compact dimensions of the Kylaq, our hotel parking was a sidewalk cordoned off by the hotel manager, as there simply was no space to park. 14th-century Gergeti Trinity Church has stunning views of the Caucasus Mountains. Still, we made the most of it by strolling by the shore of the Black Sea, watching the locals angling for fish. Georgia, just like the Stans, offered a unique glimpse into this part of the world and its diverse culture. For our final stretch before Europe, we had one last country to drive through – the colourful Türkiye. Georgia in numbers Distance covered 624km Fuel consumed 58.62 litres Average fuel economy 10.64kpl Approximate fuel cost Rs 7,607 Average per-litre fuel cost Rs 129.78 Total time driven 17.5hrs Average speed 58.5kph Türkiye – Gateway to Europe Cappadocia’s claim to fame is well worth the hype. As the Kylaq crossed into Türkiye, our first stop was in Erzurum. A major winter sports town, but thanks to the time of year, our ski resort was bright, sunny and without an ounce of snow. A quick stroll through the small town and we hit the sack in preparation for a 700km-plus drive to the tourist haven that is Cappadocia. The next morning, the plan was to do what you must do in Türkiye – take a hot-air-balloon ride. A pre-dawn wake-up call is never comfortable, but the peace was soon shattered by the sound of a group of old diesel Land Rover Defenders revving to keep themselves warm while they waited to transfer tourists to the balloon launch site. The balloon ride is arguably the largest tourist attraction in Türkiye, so there was quite the rush. We, too, loaded up the Kylaq and hit the road to get the perfect shot of the sun coming up over the hills while the sky was filled with balloons. And boy, did we get it. As the orange tinge hit the fairy chimneys, we saw what the hype was about. The visual is nothing like you have ever seen: watching one colourful hot-air balloon is rare, and here there were over a hundred. We shot GBs worth of images and videos and got back to catch up on the broken sleep from earlier. Türkiye in numbers Distance covered 1,436km Fuel consumed 98.1 litres Average fuel economy 14.63kpl Approximate fuel cost Rs 17,187 Average per-litre fuel cost Rs 134.19 Total time driven 19.5hrs Average speed 73.64kph A relaxing drive the next day got us to Istanbul, which, to some, might seem like the capital thanks to its bustling character – a glimpse of which we got as we got closer. A traffic jam stretching for more than a couple of kilometres brought the Kylaq to crawling speeds. To avoid the repercussions of driving next to hasty cab drivers, we parked the Kylaq and headed to check out the nightlife, but more importantly, the döner kebab. Exceptional interiors and an unbelievable calm in Istanbul. Similar to a shawarma, the döner kebab consists of a pile of meat that is cooked on a rotisserie over a flame. The dripping fat is mopped up by pita bread, which is then loaded with the sliced meat and seasonings. After a long walk through the Grand Bazaar, haggling for a fake Rolex, the döner becomes almost a necessity. What’s also equally stunning is the Blue Mosque. Known formally as the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, it was constructed between 1609 and 1617 in the Ottoman era by Ahmed I. To get the entire mosque in frame, you need to fall back to the Hagia Sophia Mosque, which is in the same vicinity. Both equally grand, equally detailed and equally important. The Blue Mosque, built in the Ottoman era, is majestic. To explore more of Türkiye, we got back into the Kylaq and realised there was a bridge that is unlike any other in the world. The Bosphorus Bridge is located over the Bosphorus Strait, but its claim to fame is that it, quite literally, has one end in Asia and one end in Europe. You can cross the bridge in about two minutes, depending on traffic, but the sense that you can practically drive over from Asia into Europe before you can finish watching a reel is unreal. Angling over the Bosphorus strait is a common hobby. Europe – Home Stretch Bulgaria – Romania – Hungary – Slovakia – Prague The end of our incredible Pune-to-Prague drive was now a matter of days away. After over two months on the road, we were a couple of thousand kilometres away from the finish line. The excitement that had tapered off midway was back in full force. We would be entering Europe through Bulgaria, and the border, as expected, was busy. Documentation, carnets, passports, stringent car checks and some explaining later, we were finally in. Monument of the Holy Mother of God in Haskovo. Haskovo is a quaint town with a slow pace and none of the bustle of a European city, but it boasts a Guinness record for having the towering Monument of the Holy Mother of God, the tallest statue of the Virgin Mary and Baby Jesus in the world. Naturally, we had to check it out before we headed further. Crossing countries in Europe is the equivalent of crossing states in India. There are no significant border checks or passport-control booths. A board with the blue EU flag and the name of the country is all you will see. Romania’s Arcul de Triumf an ode to the one in Paris. We crossed into Romania rather unassumingly and headed for Bucharest. The capital is picturesque and is also colloquially known as “Little Paris”. Like the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, Romania too has its own version. A tad smaller in comparison, but just as iconic. However, what takes the cake is the Parliament Building, formally known as the Palace of the Parliament, which is also the heaviest building in the world, standing at approximately a ridiculous 4,098,500 tonnes. We couldn’t verify that, but since the Kylaq looked like a mere speck in front of it, it was all the proof we needed. Bran Castle is widely marketed as Dracula’s home. Bucharest also has a thriving nightlife, with the quiet cobbled streets turning into party hubs post-sunset. As we headed towards Hungary, we couldn’t help but make a stop at Bran Castle. Despite the myth that it was once home to the famous Dracula, there is nothing but merchandise at the foot of the castle to prove that claim. Historians have dismissed the claim and, while it is fascinating, there is plenty of evidence against it. Still, that did not stop us from buying some fake vampire teeth and Dracula magnets.
